Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of melody and pitch. Check, revise, or improve work about melody and pitch using stated success criteria. Closing evidence check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about melody and pitch; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. What melody and pitch means here: Melody is an organized line of pitches heard across time; contour is the shape made by its rises, falls, and repeated tones. How the relationship changes the result: Stepwise motion often connects smoothly, leaps create sharper contrast, and repetition helps the listener recognize a phrase or arrival. Choice and tradeoff: A narrow range can feel unified but limit contrast. A wide range adds drama but may be harder to sing, play, or track accurately. Worked example: C D E G | E D C creates a rise, a high arrival, and a return; arrows or numbered steps preserve the same contour without an instrument. Non-example: Naming pitch letters without preserving their order does not show melodic contour. 1. Comparative model: Compare the supplied contrasting models for melody and pitch. Locate one shared structure and one decision that changes the effect; do not rank styles. 2. Guided practice: Complete the first supported pass on melody and pitch with the supplied model or scaffold visible. Make two short studies, keep one relationship stable, change one pitch direction, and circle the exact cue you will remove next time. 3. Independent transfer: Use melody and pitch in a new case with the model closed. State the intended effect, make or analyse the case, and cite the exact evidence that supports or challenges the intention. 4. Reflection: Compare an earlier and later state. Name the choice that changed, cite what became visible, audible, notated, or workable, and state the next revision or reason to keep the result. Your choices remain yours: Different comfortable pitch or symbol set, sound or silent notation route, contour, phrase length, final expressive change choices are valid when the learner meets objective constraints and supports the result with evidence. Use the attached Manuel Academy resource in this package. It gives you the model, example, or help sheet needed for this task. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about melody and pitch. It is part of "Elements and Principles of Art and Music". Later days in this unit cover other things, like line shape and color. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about melody and pitch; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 4, try the steps yourself before you ask for help. Give a reason in your own words for at least one choice. A labelled drawing or a spoken answer counts fully.

ATTACHED MANUEL ACADEMY LEARNER RESOURCE

Resource ID: ma-resource:ma-g4-arts-music-u01-l05

Lesson focus: melody and pitch

Resource type: ACADEMY_ORIGINAL_MODEL

MODEL B — contrasting route for melody and pitch. Reconnect: Melody is an organized line of pitches heard across time; contour is the shape made by its rises, falls, and repeated tones. Model A demonstrates: C D E G | E D C creates a rise, a high arrival, and a return; arrows or numbered steps preserve the same contour without an instrument. Model B deliberately tests the opposite pressure described here: A narrow range can feel unified but limit contrast. A wide range adds drama but may be harder to sing, play, or track accurately. Compare the two by locating pitch direction, interval size, contour, phrase, repetition, arrival, and tonal centre; do not rank them by polish or resemblance. Mark which condition makes each route useful. Then make a third small case that borrows the relationship—not the model’s subject, sequence, wording, style, or interpretation. Use it to study melody and pitch; describe evidence before judging and adapt the demonstrated relationship rather than copying a finished work.

How to use it: Use the attached Manuel Academy resource in this package. It gives you the model, example, or help sheet needed for this task.

Rights: Manuel Academy original; licensed CC BY 4.0 for learner use and adaptation. No third-party text, image, score, lyric, melody, recording, or performance is included.

Access and materials: Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available for spoken reflection, explanation, or critique and scores the same. Tap, point through, gesture, or use the supplied notation or event map without recording. A written or notated response can show structure and reasoning; it does not claim hearing or performed control that was not actually demonstrated. No instrument, microphone, camera, or public performance is required.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task uses sound (melody and pitch). You do not have to hear it to do it. You may use a written or drawn version, feel the beat by tapping or watching, or read the notes on paper instead.
Anything you have to study will also come as plain text, a described version, or a version you can touch.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
No public performance, voice recording, photo, or camera use is ever required; provide a private, written, or no-audio alternative for every task.
Use only original student work, public-domain material, or properly licensed excerpts; never reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or protected works.
The final product must remain the student’s own authorship; adult or AI assistance may support planning and feedback but must not create the graded work.

media.fallback: Count, point through, tap, speak, gesture, or read the complete pulse and pitch map silently; no instrument, speaker, microphone, or recording is required.

remediation: Route 1: Reduce melody and pitch to three locatable events, areas, steps, or decisions. Label the intended effect beside each and underline the one pitch direction relationship that should carry it. Use a separate small study, four-event loop, thumbnail, evidence table, or paper plan. The adult may model the noticing process on different material but may not change the learner’s work. Check yourself: Point to or name the exact pitch direction evidence before deciding whether it serves the intent. New attempt: Put the support away and make a new arrangement, passage, response, or plan; record what the new evidence shows. Route 2: Return to the last understandable state. Hold every relationship steady except one chosen feature from pitch direction, interval size, contour, phrase, repetition, arrival, and tonal centre; predict what that single change should do. Test the feature on scrap paper, a silent count, a two-event rehearsal loop, movable shapes, or a short evidence sentence before changing the scored work. Check yourself: Name what stayed the same, what changed, and the first observable result—without using “better” as the evidence. New attempt: Create a different small case using the same one-variable method, then transfer the finding to the original task only if it serves the learner’s intent.
extension: Apply melody and pitch under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on melody and pitch rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
